statements.text: I look forward to exploring the benefits and risks of new levels of intelligence, both artificial intelligence and genetic engineering,
statements.venue: Press release on returning to House Science Committee

statements.text: There is one issue that I think is more explosive than even the spread of nuclear weapons: engineered intelligence. By that I mean, the efforts of computer engineers and bio-engineers who may create intelligence beyond that of a human being.
statements.venue: Keynote, World Healthcare Innovation and Technology Conference

statements.text: And as we develop smarter and smarter computers, we should direct 1 or 2 percent of the effort to preventing self-awareness, ambition, self-initiative, and autonomy.
statements.venue: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee hearing

statements.text: So you could view this as a contest between the bioengineers and the computer engineers to see who will be first in developing super-intelligence. Will our successor species be carbon-based or silicon-based?
statements.venue: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee hearing

statements.text: Now, with the AI aspect, this is probably an area that we need to reinforce. [...] we need to tighten that up as well.
statements.context: Witness testimony at a House Armed Services Committee hearing on DoD IT, digital developments, and AI for fiscal year 2023.

statements.text: My line of questioning is going to be about things that won't affect us until the second half of this century. But since they relate to whether humankind will continue to be in domination of the planet Earth, they're important. [...] So my concern is what are we doing to prevent or monitor for general intelligence, self-awareness, and ambition or survival instinct?
statements.context: Congressman Brad Sherman questioning a witness at a House Subcommittee hearing on trustworthy AI, pivoting to long-term existential risks from AGI.

statements.text: Many of the products today have artificial intelligence already embedded in them.
statements.context: Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on enterprise cybersecurity for DOD information networks, featuring testimony from DOD cybersecurity officials.

statements.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is an emerging and maturing capability DOD is leveraging for enhancing warfighter capability and department operations. [...] The Department actively identifies AI components and services for supply chain risk assessment and analysis to ensure acquired components and services do not pose undue or unacceptable risk from foreign adversary influence.
statements.context: Written responses to questions from a Senate Homeland Security subcommittee hearing on DoD enterprise cybersecurity and information network protection.

statements.text:
For now #ArtificialIntelligence is a tool used by humans. Good and evil. 

But we also need to focus on decades to come when #AI, and newly engineered species, may be making their own decisions for their own purposes. (2/2)

We need to be concerned about an AI that is self-aware and ambitious. Such an AI will have risks that are beyond the apocalypse to the human race. Therefore, I propose that 10 percent of all the money we spend on AI research be used to prevent and monitor for self-awareness, volition, and ambition.
statements.context: Floor speech by Rep. Brad Sherman during House 'Issues of the Day' time, framing long-term AI and genetic engineering risks.

statements.text: AI will have dramatic effects in the short-term. It will have benefits because it is a powerful tool. It will be used by evil men and women because it is a powerful tool.

China is not going to stop developing it for the next 6 months. American corporations see big profits. They are not going to stop developing it. The private sector isn't going to spend much of its money making sure that AI is trustworthy. They are going to try to make sure that AI is profitable.

I joined @CNBC's @CNBCTheExchange to discuss the Fed interest rate decision, #Crypto, #AI and more. 

Watch the full interview ⬇️ https://t.co/0PFeCRBRPQ

How much do we accomplish by saying to an American, don't invest in an AI company in China, invest in a furniture factory in China, and then the Chinese investor, who would otherwise get the best return for investing in the furniture company, invests in AI?
statements.context: House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing on CFIUS oversight and national security investment policy.

statements.text: So, the concern is that if you incentivize an American to want to see an AI company in China do well, that American may provide the technology and the expertise, not just the capital?
statements.context: Rep. Brad Sherman questioning witnesses at a House Financial Services Committee hearing on CFIUS and national security investment screening.

statements.text: [...] the Department has long recognized the current and future AI demand for computing power and capacity. [...] We are relying on our commercial cloud service providers to deliver the needed capability, innovation, and scale to enable an AI-powered warfighter. [...] understanding that AI initiatives today are still primarily narrow but one day, will shift to that next level of intensity. We are preparing to be ready with flexible processes that allow us to securely, economically, and timely meet that need.
statements.context: DoD official testifying at a congressional hearing on technology and AI operations in the Department of Defense.

statements.text: We need to do the research so that we have the capacity to monitor for and to prevent artificial intelligence from becoming self-aware, developing volition, developing ambition, and developing a survival instinct.
statements.context: One-minute floor speech during the House 'Issues of the Day' period.

statements.text: Let us hope that artificial intelligence does not develop a survival instinct, that it does not develop self-awareness. [...] Let's take 1 percent of what we are doing to make AI more powerful to make sure it is safe. [...] What is existential is the possibility of creating an artificial intelligence with general capacities and self-learning that also happens to develop [...] self-awareness, ambition, a desire to survive, and an ability to set its own goals.
statements.context: Rep. Brad Sherman delivers remarks on the House floor about AI safety and existential risk from self-aware AI.

statements.text: We also have to think of the second half of this century and whether artificial intelligence becomes a creature with its own volition and its own objectives. [...] We had better make sure that the machines we build do not literally take on a life of their own, create their own objectives and their own tasks, seek to survive and propagate, and seek to achieve their own objectives.
statements.context: Verbatim floor remarks by Representative Brad Sherman in the House of Representatives.

statements.text: And as you are getting at from a computer science perspective, a lot of these systems are still black boxes, right. We put in A, we get B out, and we can't tell you what happened in the middle. So as much transparency as possible is good for safety reasons. It is good for ethical reasons. It is also good for security reasons because, you know, if you are trying to fix it, right, you need to understand it first.
statements.context: Verbatim remarks by Representative Brad Sherman during a Communications Networks Safety and Security hearing or briefing.

statements.text: I cannot find a program anywhere in the world—and I would support it if I could find it—designed to monitor and prevent self-awareness and ambition, to determine what can be done to prevent AI from developing its own objectives, which I think would be hostile to ours.
statements.context: Speaking at a financial services AI innovation hearing, the lawmaker questions a Google representative about AI safety and existential risk.

statements.text: there is no money in preventing AI from taking over the world. That is the next generation's problem. [...] What do you do to make sure that the prejudices of the past are not built into the computers that will control the world in the future?
statements.context: Verbatim remarks by Representative Brad Sherman during a congressional hearing on AI in financial services, questioning a Google representative about safety incentives and algorithmic discrimination.

statements.text: Can you name one person whose job it is at Google to prevent AI from becoming a creature rather than a tool?
statements.context: Remarks during a panel titled 'From Principles to Policy: Enabling 21st Century AI Innovation in Financial Services.'

statements.text: At today’s @USHouseFSC hearing, I pressed AI executives on the risk of an AI-driven market bubble, the responsibility to prevent AI from drifting toward self-awareness, and the need to ensure these systems never displace human intelligence or enable discrimination. https://t.co/PGD9nGghza

President #DonaldTrump’s decision to allow #NVIDIA to sell H200 chips to #China puts America last. 
 
U.S. companies should not be allowed to hand over to China the very technology it needs to beat America in the AI race – especially when we know that China won’t put any safeguards on AI technology.

https://t.co/d15Jk4T3o4

The Trump Administration’s reckless decision to sell advanced AI chips to China — after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang donated to Trump’s White House ballroom and attended a $1-million-a-head dinner — puts one company’s bottom line over U.S. national security and AI leadership.

We need to monitor AI to detect and prevent self-awareness and ambition. China is not the only threat. See the recent bestseller: "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All."

Whoever leads in AI may lead this century — but what if AI itself is in control?

We’re spending trillions to make AI more powerful and almost nothing to ensure it remains controllable. 

I’m pushing legislation to change that.

Learn more: https://t.co/TM0i0AkieY https://t.co/2XwnWUNojz

Right now, we are simply betting that we can make this super intelligence and that it will always do our bidding and will never have objectives of its own. We are spending nothing to monitor for or prevent that self-awareness and ambition, and we should.
statements.context: US Representative Brad Sherman delivering a one-minute floor speech in the House of Representatives about the existential risks of artificial intelligence and genetic engineering.

statements.text:
Twenty-one years ago, I delivered a @UCLA commencement address where I discussed the future of AI long before it became a household topic.

Returning to UCLA today, I revisited that same subject, examining the opportunities, risks and responsibilities.

Watch ⤵️ https://t.co/L0TGljw7jy
Our species is devoting trillions of dollars to making artificial intelligence more powerful. We're devoting basically nothing to making sure that it is controllable.

Now, I've recently introduced the most important legislation that I'll ever introduce: to fund research to build what I call the small box on top of the big box. The big box is artificial intelligence. The small box would monitor for and prevent self-awareness, ambition, survival instinct, and self-direction.

It will require us to ask not how do we beat China or other national rivals in deploying the latest technology, but rather how do we work with all nations to make sure that the power of intelligence remains a human monopoly.
Now, like many technologies, AI will make some people billionaires and more people unemployed.

Billions have been spent to create AI systems that companies know are unspeakably dangerous to us all. 

AI experts have been clear on the need to monitor for and prevent the emergence of ambitious, self aware AI systems that are rapidly emerging, and I have legislation to do just that.

statements.text:
On #MusicAdvocacyDay2026, it was good to meet with some amazingly talented music creators with the GRAMMYs @RecordingAcad. 

I’m proud to represent some of the most creative artists in the world, and they and their colleagues deserve fair compensation and property rights, particularly when AI can be used to exploit their work.

We must immediately do more to address the existential threats that dangerous AI systems already pose.

I’m leading my colleagues in urging an immediate and significant increase in funding for AI safety. 

The $15 million currently proposed for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) is ridiculously inadequate to evaluate increasingly powerful AI systems.
